title: Motor control components, terminal numbers, circuits and troubleshooting
source: Written from the ELECT 435A lab pages and general motor control practice; NFPA 79 colors from the standard.

cards.front: What is a contactor?
cards.back: A heavy-duty electrically operated switch. Its coil pulls in main power contacts that carry motor current.

cards.front: What is the difference between a contactor and a motor starter?
cards.back: A motor starter is a contactor plus an overload relay.

cards.front: What does an overload relay protect against?
cards.back: Motor overheating from sustained overcurrent. It opens the control circuit; it does not protect against short circuits.

cards.front: What protects the motor circuit against short circuits?
cards.back: The branch-circuit short-circuit and ground-fault device: fuses or a circuit breaker ahead of the starter.

cards.front: What is a control relay used for?
cards.back: Switching low-current control signals and adding contacts. It does not carry motor current.

cards.front: What does a control transformer do?
cards.back: Steps line voltage down to a safer control voltage (24 V in the lab panels) for the push buttons, coils and lights.

cards.front: What is a limit switch used for in a forward/reverse circuit?
cards.back: It opens when the machine reaches the end of travel and drops out that direction only.

cards.front: What is a pilot light for?
cards.back: Showing the operator a state, such as motor running forward.

cards.front: What does the FLA dial on an overload relay set?
cards.back: The trip current. Set it to the motor nameplate full-load amps.

cards.front: What is the difference between HAND and AUTO reset on an overload?
cards.back: HAND: someone must press reset after a trip. AUTO: it resets itself when it cools. Use HAND where an automatic restart could hurt someone.

cards.front: What are terminals A1 and A2?
cards.back: The two ends of a contactor or relay coil.

cards.front: What do 1L1, 3L2, 5L3 and 2T1, 4T2, 6T3 mean on a contactor?
cards.back: Line-side and load-side terminals of the three main power poles: 1L1 to 2T1, 3L2 to 4T2, 5L3 to 6T3.

cards.front: What do the units digits 1-2 and 3-4 tell you about an auxiliary contact?
cards.back: 1-2 is normally closed (NC); 3-4 is normally open (NO). The tens digit is the position number.

cards.front: Is aux contact 23-24 NO or NC?
cards.back: Normally open (ends in 3-4).

cards.front: Is aux contact 31-32 NO or NC?
cards.back: Normally closed (ends in 1-2).

cards.front: What are overload terminals 95-96 and 97-98?
cards.back: 95-96 is the normally closed trip contact wired in series with the coils. 97-98 is a normally open alarm contact.

cards.front: A push button's NC contact is usually numbered...?
cards.back: 1-2 (for example a STOP button).

cards.front: A push button's NO contact is usually numbered...?
cards.back: 3-4 (for example a START button).

cards.front: On an 8-pin octal relay, which pins are usually the coil?
cards.back: Pins 2 and 7.

cards.front: What do H1-H4 and X1-X4 mean on a control transformer?
cards.back: H terminals are the primary (high-voltage) side; X terminals are the secondary (low-voltage) side.

cards.front: How is a ladder diagram read?
cards.back: Left to right across each rung, top to bottom. Power rails on the sides; one load (coil or light) per rung, at the right end.

cards.front: Where do the overload contacts go in a control rung?
cards.back: In series with the coil, between the coil and the common side.

cards.front: What is a seal-in (holding) contact?
cards.back: A normally open contact of the contactor wired across the START button, so the coil stays energized after START is released.

cards.front: What is 3-wire control?
cards.back: Momentary START/STOP buttons with a seal-in contact. It gives low-voltage protection: after a power loss the motor does not restart by itself.

cards.front: What is 2-wire control?
cards.back: A maintained contact (switch, float, thermostat) runs the coil directly. It gives low-voltage release: the motor restarts when power returns.

cards.front: How are multiple STOP buttons wired?
cards.back: In series (any one opens the circuit).

cards.front: How are multiple START buttons wired?
cards.back: In parallel (any one can start).

cards.front: What does jog (inch) mean?
cards.back: The motor runs only while the button is held; the seal-in is bypassed.

cards.front: Why should a JOG circuit still be fed through STOP?
cards.back: So pressing STOP always stops the motor, even while someone is holding JOG.

cards.front: What is electrical interlocking in a forward/reverse starter?
cards.back: Each contactor's NC aux contact (for example 31-32) is wired in series with the other contactor's coil, so both can't pull in at once.

cards.front: What is mechanical interlocking?
cards.back: A mechanical bar between the two contactors that physically prevents both from closing.

cards.front: What is push-button interlocking?
cards.back: Each direction button's NC contact is in the other direction's rung, so pressing one drops out the other.

cards.front: How does a 3-phase motor reverse?
cards.back: Swap any two of the three line leads (the reversing contactor swaps L1 and L3).

cards.front: Why must forward and reverse never pull in together?
cards.back: Two lines would be shorted together phase to phase.

cards.front: What is a common forgotten wire on a starter?
cards.back: The coil return: coil A2 to the overload 95 terminal. Without it the coil has no path and nothing pulls in.

cards.front: NFPA 79 wire color for AC control circuits?
cards.back: Red.

cards.front: NFPA 79 wire color for DC control circuits?
cards.back: Blue.

cards.front: NFPA 79 wire color for the grounded (common) control conductor?
cards.back: White (or white with a stripe for DC).

cards.front: NFPA 79 wire color for equipment grounding?
cards.back: Green, or green with yellow stripe.

cards.front: What color does NFPA 79 use for interlock circuits fed from an outside source?
cards.back: Orange (or yellow), because they stay live when the panel disconnect is off.

cards.front: Why should a white wire be used only for the grounded conductor?
cards.back: Workers assume white is near ground potential. A white wire upstream of the overload contact can read full control voltage when the overload trips.

cards.front: Why is one side of the control transformer secondary grounded?
cards.back: So a ground fault in the control circuit blows the fuse or trips the breaker instead of starting the motor by itself.

cards.front: Which side of the control circuit goes to the push buttons and contacts?
cards.back: The fused, ungrounded (hot) side. The grounded side goes to the coils' A2 ends through the overload contacts.

cards.front: Why give every wire a number at both ends?
cards.back: So the panel matches the ladder diagram and anyone can trace a fault.

cards.front: What must be off before doing ohm or continuity checks on a control panel?
cards.back: All power: cord unplugged, motor supply unplugged, control breaker off.

cards.front: Why are continuity checks useless with the control transformer still connected and switched on?
cards.back: The transformer secondary joins the hot and common buses through a few ohms, so almost everything reads continuous.

cards.front: What should a contactor coil read on an ohmmeter?
cards.back: A definite resistance: not zero (shorted) and not open.

cards.front: How do you bench-test a contactor's main contacts without power?
cards.back: Push the armature in by hand and check each pole (1L1-2T1 and so on) goes from open to continuous.

cards.front: A motor starts but stops as soon as START is released. Most likely cause?
cards.back: The seal-in (holding) contact is missing, miswired or not closing.

cards.front: Pressing START does nothing at all. What do you check first?
cards.back: Control power, the STOP button and overload contact (both NC), and the coil return wire.

cards.front: An overload keeps tripping. What are common causes?
cards.back: FLA set too low, a mechanically overloaded or binding motor, a lost phase (single-phasing), or a bad connection heating the overload.

cards.front: What is single-phasing?
cards.back: Losing one line of a 3-phase supply. The motor draws high current on the other two lines and overheats.

cards.front: What is the safe way to check for voltage?
cards.back: Test your meter on a known live source, test the circuit, then test the meter again (live-dead-live).
